extracted.intended_audience: literate public; poets, writers, and readers interested in literary criticism and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for epic/heroic poets about appropriate sentiments, tone, and the use (or avoidance) of humor, with related advice about diction vs sentiment; the essay also gives social/conversational maxims relevant to character and dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnatural or affected thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: "An Epic Poet should not only avoid such Sentiments as are unnatural or affected" (i.e., avoid thoughts that seem forced or artificial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the poem's ideas and feelings believable within its world and characters; avoid courting novelty for its own sake. Anti-patterns: contrived conceits or affected philosophical turns that break the epic's gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mean and vulgar sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poets must avoid "such as are mean and vulgar" — low or groveling thoughts even if they may be natural in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low, grovelling, or petty sentiments undermine the heroic/noble register of epic. Note: Homer has some homely passages explained as simplicity of age, but the guideline is to exclude mean/vulgar thought from an epic's dominant tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor that raises laughter seldom fits heroic/epic poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sentiments which raise Laughter, can very seldom be admitted with any Decency into an Heroic Poem, whose Business it is to excite Passions of a much nobler Nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer stirring, noble passions over comic effect in epic passages. Examples of lapses: Homer (characters like Vulcan, Thersites, Irus) provide burlesque moments that critics have attacked; include such instances only sparingly and with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a serious air; avoid burlesque character
rubrics_metrics.description: The burlesque character "departs from that serious Air which seems essential to the Magnificence of an Epic Poem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained burlesque or mockery weakens an epic's grandeur. If any comic or grotesque episode is included, it must not overturn the poem's overall majestic tone; if it does, it becomes an imperfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual appropriateness and timing of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor may be allowable depending on context—e.g., the Aeneid's single laugh in Book 5 is acceptable because it occurs in the "Book of Games and Diversions" where readers are relaxed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the narrative moment permits relaxation of tone; well-timed, contextually-placed levity can be permissible. Scoring note: humor is more defensible in explicitly playful or episodic sections than in central, tragic, or climactic passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns and trivial pleasantry are objectionable in serious epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages consisting of a "String of Punns" (as in the cited Milton passage) are "the most exceptionable" in a serious poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cheap wordplay or sustained punning in elevated passages; such devices are anti-patterns for maintaining epic dignity and can be singled out as weakness by severe critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Sentiment (content) from Diction (words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Aristotle: Sentiments = the object/content of speech (what is said); Diction = the words themselves (how it is said).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and craft both levels separately: ensure the underlying sentiment suits the work's moral/tonal aims, and then choose diction that supports that sentiment. The footnote reminds writers to treat content and expression as distinct but related concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity is essential to pleasing others
rubrics_metrics.description: "The happy Talent of Pleasing... seems to be wholly owing to the Opinion they have of your Sincerity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing characters or crafting narrative voice intended to charm, ground that charm in perceived sincerity rather than obvious performance. In dialogue, readers (like social peers) respond to apparent honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreeable conversation flows from delicacy of sentiment and chastity of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: "A rational and select Conversation is composed of Persons, who have the Talent of Pleasing with Delicacy of Sentiments flowing from habitual Chastity of Thought."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For realistic, likable dialogue or character behavior, give speakers restrained, refined sentiments rooted in consistent moral/mental habits; avoid characters whose 'agreeableness' is merely surface acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pretended mirth and constrained/obscene witticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed company is "pestered with constrained, obscene, and painful Witticisms" from pretenders to mirth — a social anti-pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dialogue and social scenes, avoid forced jokes, crude one-liners, or witticisms that feel embarrassing rather than genuinely amusing; such lines ring false and reduce character credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation/acknowledged merit lends weight to ordinary behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Known merit or past conspicuous actions make otherwise indifferent behaviour seem graceful and important (e.g., Polycarpus' past gallantry lends dignity to trivial acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character backstory and reputation can be used as a tool: a character's history should inflect how readers interpret present actions. In evaluating scenes, consider how established reputation changes perceived import.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ingratiate by mimicking a patron's manner (avoid parasitical flattery)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Falling in with the particular Humour or Manner of one above you... is the Life of a Slave. A Parasite differs in nothing from the meanest Servant... the other gives up his very Soul."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a moral/character guideline, avoid characters who succeed solely by sycophancy; such behavior is presented as degrading. For authors, sincere alignment of character voice with other characters is preferable to transparent mimicry for advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importunity; speak modestly of your wants
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace's admonitions: avoid importunity and "speak Modestly of your own Wants"; shameless self-exposure repels sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters who constantly advertise needs or beg are unsympathetic; in narrative, modesty of appeal makes a plea more persuasive. Anti-pattern: the 'beggar who exposes his sores'—it repels rather than moves others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be as little troublesome as possible; present requests as favors rather than claims
rubrics_metrics.description: "The main Art is to be as little troublesome as you can, and make all you hope for come rather as a Favour from your Patron than Claim from you."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In crafting scenes of supplication or negotiation, show characters minimizing imposition and framing asks tactfully. This is practical social rhetoric useful for believable courtship, patronage, or plea scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two means of gaining from others: be agreeable or be useful/considerable
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are but two Means in the World of gaining by other Men, and these are by being either agreeable or considerable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing character strategies for advancement, choose whether a character relies on charm/agreeableness or on actual service/value. This distinction is a useful axis for plot and character motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thrift, diligence, and method as ways to practical success (on worldly conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical means to grow a fortune are listed as: thrift, diligence, and method in business; these are attainable virtues for most people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not a literary rule, these maxims inform realistic character motivations and social milieus: authors portraying social mobility should reflect such pragmatic virtues. Anti-pattern: mistaking every unusual success for mere 'genius'—the essay cautions realistic attribution of outcomes.
